<reason>A ran a sophisticated over-inclusion case: by embracing enforceable honest totals, prominent material restrictions, and pre-commitment review, A credibly neutralized B's headline $420-to-$660 drip-pricing example and exposed B's occasional attacks on a strawman checkout. But B's surviving route was stronger. The house-rules/classification point ("who decides what's material — the host who profits") was never fully escaped: A's objective-standard answer concedes exactly the screen-by-screen enforcement burden B's bright line avoids. B also minimized the mandate's cost (the same stored text, one click earlier, on the same small screen A calls intelligible at review), landed a genuine fork in B4.2, and closed with clean error-asymmetry weighing — redundancy if the mandate is wrong versus legally gated disclosure if A's patchwork fails. A's late hits (conspicuousness is itself a judgment; the funnel boundary needs interpretation) narrowed but did not close that administrability gap, and A's residual attention-dilution cost was modest. Both sides executed the Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 format cleanly and stayed epistemically disciplined; B's rhetoric ("one judgment, made once," "draw the line where walking away is still free") consistently sharpened the actual decision rule rather than substituting for it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 to Rebuttal 2 sequence on house rules: the overload "refutes itself" point plus the pressure question "who decides materiality?" forced A into an enforceable objective-standard answer, which B's closing then outflanked with the bright-line-versus-litigated-bundle weighing. A's best counter — that B's own conspicuousness standard also requires judgment — came too late and only narrowed the gap rather than eliminating it.</best_rebuttal>
